newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban said routing opposition.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban said routing opposition.

text.p: Islamic Taleban warriors swept through northern Afghanistan on Sunday, ousting opposition forces from three more provincial capitals, Afghan and Pakistan-based sources said on Sunday.

This northern capital, the last major city to hold out against the Taleban, appeared to be under the full control of ethnic Uzbek fighters who had until last week been part of an alliance opposing the purist Islamic movement.

Taleban official Mullah Wakhil Ahmed Motawakhil told Reuters in Kabul the towns of Kunduz and Baghlan east of Mazar came under Taleban control when fighters from one faction in the alliance switched sides.

"Former Hezb-i-Islami fighters in Kunduz and Baghlan have joined the Taleban and the towns are now under their control." said Motawakhil, speaking by telephone from the Taleban's headquarters in the city of Kandahar.
The Pakistan-based Afghan news service said the provinces of Kunduz and Baghlan and nearby Samangan province, including its capital Aibak, had fallen to the Taleban on Sunday.
There was no independent confirmation of the reports.
The provinces and towns lie east of the city of Mazar-i-Sharif, headquarters of northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum until its dramatic capture by the Taleban on Saturday.

The Taleban advance ends an eight-month deadlock between the purist Islamic movement and a fragile coalition linking Dostum with former government forces of Burhanuddin Rabbani, Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami and the mainly Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat.
The coalition's defences fell apart when Dostum's key commander, General Abdul Malik, defected to the Taleban last Monday, exposing the alliance's western flank.
The Taleban sweep has left the alliance in tatters and stranded from supply lines in the Hindu Kush mountains.
A Shi'ite Moslem militia was still offering resistance in the central city of Bamiyan, while former government military commander Ahmed Shah Masood holds part of the north east.
Dostum is believed to have fled, possibly to neighbouring Uzbekistan, but there was no firm word on his whereabouts.
"Dostum has fled to an unidentified location with his family and KGB comrades." said an aide to Malik, referring to Dostum's past association with the communists.

There was no immediate word from Afghanistan's neighbours on the dramatic takeover. Pakistan has backed the Taleban since its emergence in 1994 but Iran and former Soviet states bordering Afghanistan have supported Dostum, seeing him as a buffer.

Russia said on Saturday on the situation had severely worsened and warned that any violation of international borders would trigger a speedy response from the Commonwealth of Independent States, successor organisation to the Soviet Union.

In Mazar ethnic Uzbek fighters loyal to General Malik consolidated control over Dostum's former stronghold, tearing down a huge portrait of ex-leader Dostum when they arrived, replacing it with Malik's.
Malik, Dostum's former foreign minister, has been named deputy foreign minister in the Taleban government in Kabul.
White flags, emblem of the purist Taleban Islamic militia, fluttered from the rebels' vehicles, although the fighters all appeared to be northerners.
Crowds of civilians, almost all men and boys, milled around in the streets, but shops remained shuttered, market stalls were empty and there were no private cars in sight.
Malik forces were also in control of Dostum's base at Qala-i-Jhangi (fortress of war), a vast mud walled citadel about 20 km (13 miles) southwest of Mazar-i-Sharif.
